idiom_name: func(T) bool values with closures; generic combinator helpers since Go 1.18
implementation_notes: A rule is an ordinary function value - `type Spec[T any] func(T) bool` - so the class hierarchy collapses into closures, and And/Or/Not are small generic functions returning new function values with short-circuit evaluation. Collections consume predicates directly through a hand-written Filter[T] helper or a loop; the standard library has no generic filter, so the combinator set is project-local. The interface form (`type Spec[T any] interface { IsSatisfiedBy(T) bool }`) is still justified when the rule is a named domain concept that must sit in a registry, be logged, or be translated into SQL by hand - Go's database code builds query strings/arguments, so the translator exists either way and is usually the reason to keep a named type.
pitfalls: There is no composition operator for predicates: every combinator is hand-written (or vendored), and each layer adds one indirect call per candidate - visible in tight loops.
Closures capture by reference, so a rule closing over a loop variable or a mutated struct field changes meaning; bind the value explicitly before capturing.
Generics require Go 1.18 and the standard library still has no generic Filter, so older code duplicates typed helpers or falls back to interface{} plus type assertions, losing compile-time safety.
Function values are not comparable: Specifications cannot be map keys or compared with ==, so rules cannot be deduplicated by value.
